Series::traverse_put_¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::traverse_put_(pluss::RangeView<ExtractSpec> specs, const Series& values) -> Series&

What It Does¶

Writes into the current Series through a selector that must stay view-representable, mutates in place, and returns the same handle.

This is the write-side companion to traverse_slice(). It accepts dynamic selector syntax, but only the subset that can still be lowered into ordinary view operations such as selecting, slicing, and inserting a logical axis marker.

That restriction is not an accident. It is the reason to choose the method at all. traverse_put_() gives you selector-based writes while still guarding against drifting into masked or gathered writes that would need materialized destination positions.

Parameters¶

specs (pluss::RangeView<ExtractSpec>)

The destination selector.

Accepted selector forms are the same view-representable subset used by traverse_slice():

  • scalar indices

  • positive-step slices

  • SliceAll()

  • Ellipsis()

  • NewAxis()

Rejected selector forms include:

  • negative-step slices

  • bool masks

  • integer index Series

  • any mixed selector that requires advanced materialization

NewAxis() is still legal because it is shape bookkeeping, not a new writable destination dimension.

values (const Series&)

The source values to write into the selected destination region.

Two value modes are accepted:

  • scalar source: broadcast across every selected destination element

  • non-scalar source: element count must exactly match the selected destination element count

This is a stricter selector gate than extract_put_(), not a different write-cardinality model.

Returns¶

Series& The same Series, after mutation.

Examples¶

Example 1. Shared setup. Start from a simple 3 x 4 grid.

auto grid = pluss::make_series({
    {10.0, 11.0, 12.0, 13.0},
    {20.0, 21.0, 22.0, 23.0},
    {30.0, 31.0, 32.0, 33.0},
});

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[10, 11, 12, 13],
  [20, 21, 22, 23],
  [30, 31, 32, 33]]

Example 2. A whole-column write is accepted because the destination remains a plain view.

grid.traverse_put_(
    {pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(), std::int64_t{1}},
    pluss::make_series({100.0, 200.0, 300.0}));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[10, 100, 12, 13],
  [20, 200, 22, 23],
  [30, 300, 32, 33]]

Example 3. NewAxis() is accepted here too. It participates in selector normalization, but it does not create a new writable destination dimension.

grid.traverse_put_(
    {pluss::Slicing::NewAxis(), pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(), std::int64_t{0}},
    pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 100, 12, 13],
  [2, 200, 22, 23],
  [3, 300, 32, 33]]

Example 4. Scalar broadcast still works after the stricter selector gate has accepted the destination.

grid.traverse_put_(
    {std::int64_t{2}, pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(2, 4, 1)},
    pluss::make_series(-5.0));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 100, 12, 13],
  [2, 200, 22, 23],
  [3, 300, -5, -5]]

Example 5. Ellipsis() is also part of the accepted view-representable subset.

grid.traverse_put_(
    {pluss::Slicing::Ellipsis(), std::int64_t{3}},
    pluss::make_series({13.5, 23.5, 33.5}));

std::cout << grid;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=12, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 100, 12, 13.5],
  [2, 200, 22, 23.5],
  [3, 300, -5, 33.5]]

Example 6. Reverse slices are rejected because they are not view-representable on this stricter surface.

try {
  grid.traverse_put_(
      {pluss::Slicing::SliceAll(), pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(-1, pluss::Slicing::Slice::kUnbounded, -1)},
      pluss::make_series(0.0));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

Series::traverse_put_: selector is not view-representable; use extract() or extract_put_() for materializing paths

Example 7. Bool masks are rejected for the same reason.

try {
  auto row_mask = pluss::make_series({true, false, true});
  grid.traverse_put_(
      {row_mask, pluss::Slicing::SliceAll()},
      pluss::make_series(0.0));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

Series::traverse_put_: selector is not view-representable; use extract() or extract_put_() for materializing paths

Example 8. Cardinality mismatches still fail, and the message bubbles from the shared selector-write machinery.

try {
  grid.traverse_put_(
      {std::int64_t{0}, pluss::Slicing::SliceRange(0, 2, 1)},
      pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

Series::extract_put_: source must be scalar or match selected element count

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • traverse_put_() is strict by design. If a selector would require materialized advanced indexing, this method rejects it.

  • NewAxis() is accepted, but it is only a normalization marker, not a new writable dimension.

  • Reverse slices, bool masks, and integer index Series are all disallowed here even though extract_put_() can handle them.

  • Some validation errors still mention extract_put_() because both methods share the same underlying write-cardinality checks after selector admission.

Summary¶

Choose traverse_put_() when you want selector-language writes but you also want the API to enforce “stay in ordinary view territory.” It is the strict in-place sibling of traverse_slice(). The moment your selector needs masks, reverse traversal, or advanced integer selection, switch to extract_put_().
